Marine macroalgae, surrounding seawater, and surrounding sediment were collected at Weihai, China (122.12 N, 37.56 E). Phycosphere bacteria: Macroalgae were cut into pieces and rinsed thrice with sterile seawater. Afterwards, 10 g of these pieces were washed with 10 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C). One-milliliter aliquots were diluted stepwise to 1:100,000 (sterile seawater), and 100 μl were subsequently plated and incubated (21 d, 28 °C). Seawater samples: One-milliliter seawater was diluted stepwise with 9 ml sterile seawater to 1:1,000. Aliquots of 100 μl were then plated and incubated as described above. Sediment samples: Sediment samples of 1 g were thoroughly mixed with 9 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C) and then diluted in 1:10 steps with sterile seawater to 1:10,000. Afterwards, 100 μl aliquots were plated. Two media were used for plating, modified 2216E and modified VY/2 medium. Plating was completed within 2 h after sampling. After incubation, colony-forming units were counted with numbers ranging from 10 to 500. Colonies were selected depending on color, size, and shape. Picked colonies were purified by serial cultivation on plates with identical media. Purified strains were stored at -80 °C in a sterile 1% (w/v) saline medium with 15% (v/v) glycerol.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: This project provides the whole genome sequence of Bacillus anthracis isolated from the water samples of Badi Lake, an urban freshwater body in Udaipur, Rajasthan, India. The sample was specifically collected during the winter season to study the microbial diversity and the spread of antibiotic resistance in freshwater environments. As the isolate exhibits an antimicrobial-resistant phenotype, this genomic data will be used to identify specific antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors, and mobile genetic elements. This study contributes to the understanding of environmental reservoirs of resistance and the genomic characterization of the genus Bacillus in diverse ecological niches.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: In an effort to better understand how Bacillus cereus 03BB102 acquires multidrug resistance, we examined the organisms response to elevated levels of different antibiotics (tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and vancomycin). Illumina and PacBio sequencing of the isolates and comparing them to the parental strain helped us to identify genomic changes during the stepwise in vitro generation of multidrug resistant isolates.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: Botrytis cinerea is one of the most serious fungal phytopathogens attacking hemp and cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.). The restricted use of chemical fungicides in cannabis cultivation promotes research for alternatives, such as those derived from microbes. Bacteria isolated from crude oil-dwelling bacteria tend to produce biosurfactants (BSs), the well-known antifungal compounds. Using hemp seed oil as a possible hydrophobic nich, we isolated and screened several potential biocontrols that significantly inhibited Botrytis mycelium in vitro, including Bacillus mojavensis HOB3.
We want to study the biocontrol mechanism of B. mojavensis Bai2-32.

Marine macroalgae, surrounding seawater, and surrounding sediment were collected at Weihai, China (122.12 N, 37.56 E). Phycosphere bacteria: Macroalgae were cut into pieces and rinsed thrice with sterile seawater. Afterwards, 10 g of these pieces were washed with 10 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C). One-milliliter aliquots were diluted stepwise to 1:100,000 (sterile seawater), and 100 μl were subsequently plated and incubated (21 d, 28 °C). Seawater samples: One-milliliter seawater was diluted stepwise with 9 ml sterile seawater to 1:1,000. Aliquots of 100 μl were then plated and incubated as described above. Sediment samples: Sediment samples of 1 g were thoroughly mixed with 9 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C) and then diluted in 1:10 steps with sterile seawater to 1:10,000. Afterwards, 100 μl aliquots were plated. Two media were used for plating, modified 2216E and modified VY/2 medium. Plating was completed within 2 h after sampling. After incubation, colony-forming units were counted with numbers ranging from 10 to 500. Colonies were selected depending on color, size, and shape. Picked colonies were purified by serial cultivation on plates with identical media. Purified strains were stored at -80 °C in a sterile 1% (w/v) saline medium with 15% (v/v) glycerol.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: Mastitis, the inflammation of the mammary gland, is one of the most frequent diseases of dairy animals and a leading cause of economic losses to farmers and the dairy industry. Mastitis is also one of the main reasons for antibiotic use in dairy farms contributing to the development and spread of antibiotic resistance through the food chain. Here, we describe a pipeline for developing a probiotic, biofilm-inspired alternative for mastitis prevention. We isolated and characterized putative probiotic bacteria from healthy cows udders without a history of mastitis. We subsequently identified two promising isolates Bacillus subtilis O4 and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum V1, with complementary properties. L. plantarum V1 showed potent inhibition of mastitis-causing pathogens via soluble and volatile compounds that were further identified. Induced biofilm formation by B. subtilis O4 enabled the development of an encapsulation system to protect L. plantarum V1 in environmental conditions. When combined cultures of both strains were applied in vivo as a probiotic teat dipping formulation, L. plantarum V1 showed excellent survival on the teat skin and altered the residing microbiota. We propose a novel natural probiotic treatment that can potentially be used in mastitis control.

Marine macroalgae, surrounding seawater, and surrounding sediment were collected at Weihai, China (122.12 N, 37.56 E). Phycosphere bacteria: Macroalgae were cut into pieces and rinsed thrice with sterile seawater. Afterwards, 10 g of these pieces were washed with 10 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C). One-milliliter aliquots were diluted stepwise to 1:100,000 (sterile seawater), and 100 μl were subsequently plated and incubated (21 d, 28 °C). Seawater samples: One-milliliter seawater was diluted stepwise with 9 ml sterile seawater to 1:1,000. Aliquots of 100 μl were then plated and incubated as described above. Sediment samples: Sediment samples of 1 g were thoroughly mixed with 9 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C) and then diluted in 1:10 steps with sterile seawater to 1:10,000. Afterwards, 100 μl aliquots were plated. Two media were used for plating, modified 2216E and modified VY/2 medium. Plating was completed within 2 h after sampling. After incubation, colony-forming units were counted with numbers ranging from 10 to 500. Colonies were selected depending on color, size, and shape. Picked colonies were purified by serial cultivation on plates with identical media. Purified strains were stored at -80 °C in a sterile 1% (w/v) saline medium with 15% (v/v) glycerol.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: A new Tunisian Bacillus thuringiensis strain, shows an important larvicidal activity against mosquitoes larvae. It could be very useful and an effective alternative for mosquitoes control, implying its possible exploitation in pest management programs. The genome sequence of BLB406 strain was obtained using miSeq Illumina next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology. BLB406 was a novel B. thuringiensis strain harbouring 5 cry genes (cry11, cry22, cry42, cry60 and cry64) different from the published ones and one vegetative insecticidal protein gene (vip4). The isolation of new B. thuringiensis strains having a novel combination of toxins may resolve some problems such as the narrow insecticidal spectra and insect resistance.

Assembly BioSample Description Title: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens isolated from seeds of wheat cultivar Kanchan
Assembly BioSample Description Comment: Wheat blast, caused by a fungus Magnaporthe oryzae Triticum pathotype, has been a threat to wheat production in Brazil and some countries in South America since its first emergence in Parana state of Brazil in 1985. In February 2016, it emerged for the first time in Bangladesh and devastated more than 15,000 hectares of wheat in a large area of the South-western and western parts of Bangladesh. At present, it is unclear whether resistant wheat varieties against M. oryzae are available and the degree to which fungicide application for the neck blast management is reliable. Applications of plant probiotic bacteria are known to promote growth of host plants and suppress phytopathogenic fungi by various mechanisms. However, there are no biocontrol agents so far developed against the wheat blast fungus. To find potential biocontrol agents, we screened several hundreds of plant probiotic bacteria isolated from the surface sterilized seeds and organs of various crop plants including wheat and rice in Bangladesh. Some of the isolates including Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain BTLK6A displayed potent inhibitory activities against the wheat blast fungus in vitro and suppression of disease in vivo. We sequenced this bacterial isolate and assembled the genome using the services provided by MicrobesNG.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: Root-knot nematodes (RKNs; Meloidogyne spp.), as one of the most economically important plant-parasitic nematodes (PPNs), cause severe yield and quality losses in agriculture annually. Application of beneficial rhizobacterium like Bacillus genus is an environmental-safely and effective alternative to control RKNs. Here, we isolated a Bacillus velezensis strain YS-AT-DS1 (Bv-DS1) from the tidal soil. In vitro laboratory assays indicated that Bv-DS1 displayed the obvious antifugal activities against Rhizoctonia solani, Fusarium avenaceum and Fusarium graminearum, as well as the nematicidal activity against Meloidogyne incognita. Thus, Bv-DS1 strain could be used to exploit a biocontrol agent for RKN control in sustainable agriculture.

Assembly BioSample Description Comment: The strain Bacillus velezensis UCMB-5139 exhibits a high level of antagonistic activity against S. aureus, E. coli, P. vulgaris, and several fungal cultures. It synthesizes a complex of extracellular bacteriolytic and yeast-lytic enzymes, as well as amino acids, exopolysaccharides, and phenolic compounds with antioxidant and antiradical activity. From the culture fluid supernatant of the strains, complex enzyme complexes with a broad spectrum of protease activity have been isolated: fibrinolytic and caseinolytic enzymes, elastase, and collagenase. An activation of the phagocytic activity of leukocytes and macrophages by this strain has been reported. It is used as a component of a for veterinary probiotic for the treatment and prevention of dysbiosis; intestinal and purulent infections; and postpartum endometritis in animals. Publications: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12602-021-09827-y and https://doi.org/10.15407/microbiolj86.05.003.

Marine macroalgae, surrounding seawater, and surrounding sediment were collected at Weihai, China (122.12 N, 37.56 E). Phycosphere bacteria: Macroalgae were cut into pieces and rinsed thrice with sterile seawater. Afterwards, 10 g of these pieces were washed with 10 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C). One-milliliter aliquots were diluted stepwise to 1:100,000 (sterile seawater), and 100 μl were subsequently plated and incubated (21 d, 28 °C). Seawater samples: One-milliliter seawater was diluted stepwise with 9 ml sterile seawater to 1:1,000. Aliquots of 100 μl were then plated and incubated as described above. Sediment samples: Sediment samples of 1 g were thoroughly mixed with 9 ml sterile seawater (rotary shaker, 170 rpm., 30 min, 25 °C) and then diluted in 1:10 steps with sterile seawater to 1:10,000. Afterwards, 100 μl aliquots were plated. Two media were used for plating, modified 2216E and modified VY/2 medium. Plating was completed within 2 h after sampling. After incubation, colony-forming units were counted with numbers ranging from 10 to 500. Colonies were selected depending on color, size, and shape. Picked colonies were purified by serial cultivation on plates with identical media. Purified strains were stored at -80 °C in a sterile 1% (w/v) saline medium with 15% (v/v) glycerol.
